title: Coyne Flats Community Association
description: The community association for Coyne Flats, a settlement of 400 at the end of the branch line: the hall, the August chicken barbecue, the depot that stood from 1898 to 1987, and a links page last checked in January 2011.

blocks.text: *** COYNE FLATS COMMUNITY ASSOCIATION *** THE HALL, THE CEMETERY, THE FLAGS AND THE CHICKEN *** MEETINGS FIRST MONDAY AT SEVEN *** CHICKEN BARBECUE SECOND SATURDAY IN AUGUST ***

blocks.caption: The hall on Sarles Road, October 2006, after the west slope was done. It was the Coyne Flats School from 1927 to 1961. The bell is not in the belfry any more. The bell is in the entry where somebody can see it.

blocks.body:
Coyne Flats is not a village. There is no mayor, no village board and no village clerk, and there never has been one. We are a settlement in the [b]Town of Cobb[/b], eleven and a half miles east of Marchfield at the end of what used to be the branch line. The town office is at Cobb Corners and the supervisor is there Tuesday mornings.

The Association exists because somebody has to hang the flags, keep a roof on the hall, cut the grass at the cemetery and cook the chicken. It was organised in 1949 as the Coyne Flats Improvement Club and incorporated under its present name in 1963, which was the year we bought the school.

[b]Dues are $5 a household for the year[/b], $3 if everybody in the house is over seventy. 118 households paid for 2009. Nobody has ever been kept out of the hall or off the chicken line for not paying, and that is not going to change.

We mail a one-page bulletin three times a year: in March, in July with the barbecue tickets, and at the end of November. If you have moved and you want it, tell the secretary.

rows: First Monday of the month, 7:00 p.m. No meeting in July or August.
Anybody. You do not have to be a member to come and you do not have to be a member to say something.
First Monday in November. Officers are elected there.
Nine. Fourteen in March, when the hall rates are set.
Read at the next meeting and kept in a binder on the shelf in the hall. They are not on this site and there is no plan to put them on it.

items: [url=/depot]The depot[/url] -- the building that stood at the end of track from 1898 to 1987, with the dates, the agents and what is left on the ground.
[url=/barbecue]The chicken barbecue[/url] -- when it is, what it costs, how the day goes, and the sauce, written out so we can stop copying it onto envelopes.

[url=/officers]Officers[/url] -- who they are, what the committees are, the dues, and the treasurer's figures.
[url=/links]Links[/url] -- other pages in this county. Several of them have stopped answering and we have left them on.

blocks.body:
[b]27 December 2009.[/b] Chad is home for the week. He put the 2009 barbecue figures on, corrected the officers after the November meeting, and took the guestbook off and then put it back on.

This site is typed out by Dorothy Wenzel and put on the machine by her grandson Chad, who is at school in Bowes City and is here at Christmas and in August. That is when it changes. If something on here is out of date the rest of the year, that is the reason. He says he can do it from there. He has done it from there twice.

[b]About the internet out here.[/b] Most of us are on dial-up and the ones who are not are on a satellite dish and are not happy about it. The Town of Cobb put its name on an application for a line out this way in 2005 and again in 2008, both times with Nye Mills and Dorrance, and both times it did not get funded. The Association wrote a letter of support both times and the second letter was the first letter with the date changed.

We are told there will be a third application.

The counter was put on in 2001 and it was reset by accident in 2005 when the site was moved. Whatever it says, halve it, and then take off a few hundred for Chad checking that the site still comes up.

blocks.body:
We applied to the Gridfall Webring in March 2004. Mrs. Vance wrote back the same week and said she had us and would put us in at the next add. We are not on her member list. We have not written again, because she checks every link in that ring by hand with a notepad and she does it for nothing, and one more letter from us is not what that job needs.

The code below was copied off the bottom of Marion Teale's page in 2004, which means the PREVIOUS and the NEXT on it are hers and not ours. Chad says he will fix it. He said that in 2006.

There is no depot at Coyne Flats. There has not been one since 1987, and the ball field is still called the freight house field, which is where most of the confusion starts.

This page is what the Association has been able to put together out of the scrapbook, a map the Society in Marchfield sent us, the timetable in the case in the hall entry, and two people's memories. Where we are not sure we have said so, and where somebody has corrected us we have said that too, at the bottom.

blocks.caption: The track side, about 1962. The bay is the part sticking out under the three windows and that is where the agent sat so he could see both ways up the track. The freight door is open because it was always open in the summer. The car is somebody's and we have had four different names for it.

rows: The Marchfield & Coyne Valley Railroad is chartered. Five of the eleven subscribers are from here. Their names are on a printed prospectus in the scrapbook and four of those families are still here.
First train to the end of track, 11 November. There is no building yet. The office is a boxcar body on blocks with a stove in it.
The depot is built. Frame, on a stone foundation, with the bay on the track side.
The line is sold to the Verity & Ardo Railway.
The valuation map is made. It calls the building Station, frame, 24 x 62, fair.
Passenger service goes from two trains a day each way to one mixed train.
Last scheduled passenger train, Saturday 26 September.
The agency closes, 30 June. After this the building is a freight house and everybody starts calling it one.
The order board comes down. The mast stays until 1974.
The waiting room benches go to the grange, where two of them still are.
The co-op puts up its own fertilizer building on the far side of the platform.
Verity Rail Company takes over the line.
The roof goes over the freight room in the winter and is not repaired.
The building is burned by the fire company as a training exercise, Saturday 17 October.
Last car in to this end. A covered hopper of dry fertilizer, 4 October.
Last movement on the branch, Friday 14 March. It did not come down here. See below.

blocks.body:
Twenty-four feet by sixty-two, frame, board and batten, painted the railroad's yellow with brown trim and then painted grey in 1954 because the yellow paint had been discontinued and nobody was going to mix it.

Three rooms. The [b]waiting room[/b] at the east end, with a stove in the middle of it and a bench on three walls. The [b]office[/b] in the middle, with the bay window on the track side so the agent could see up and down the line, the telegraph table, the ticket window into the waiting room, and a safe that went to the Marchfield yard in 1958 and has not been heard of since. The [b]freight room[/b] at the west end, two thirds of the building, with a sliding door on each side and a platform scale set into the floor.

The platform was concrete on the track side, put in about 1926 over the original plank, and cinders everywhere else. There was a two-hole privy behind it until 1957. There was never running water in the building and there was never a telephone in it until 1948.
Seven men held the agency in sixty years and we have five of them for certain. The gap is 1906, and if anybody has anything at all on the man between Ferrel and Rask we would like to see it.

head: AGENT
YEARS
rows: The first. Came off the Ardo line and went back to it. Signed the first freight bill, which the Society has and which we do not.
Somebody was here for most of a year. A name that may be Vosburg appears twice in the scrapbook in different hands.

Died in the influenza in November 1919. His wife Anna kept the office six weeks until the railroad sent a man, and was not paid for it. There is a carbon in the scrapbook of a letter she wrote to the superintendent about it, and no reply.
Twenty-two years, which is the longest. Kept the record book that has the car numbers in it.
The war years. Went to the Marchfield yard afterward and retired off it in 1971.
The last agent. Went to the co-op when the agency closed and kept its books until 1974. President of this Association from 1956 to 1963 and the man who put in the bid for the school.

blocks.body:
The timetable in the case in the hall entry is dated 29 April 1949 and it is the only one anybody here has. It is a folder for the whole Marchfield district and this end of it is eleven lines.

By then it was one mixed train each way, No. 15 up and No. 16 down, and mixed means it did the freight work on the way and took as long as it took. If you had to be somewhere at a particular hour you drove, and by 1949 nearly everybody did.

The fare to Marchfield in 1949 was thirty-five cents. Before 1929 it was two trains a day each way and a Saturday evening train in the summer that came back at eleven, which is the one people's grandmothers talk about and which is the reason the older people in this village all seem to have met somebody at a dance in Marchfield.

The last scheduled passenger train was Saturday 26 September 1953. The [url=synth://verityledger.com/]Ledger[/url] of 30 September gave it three inches on an inside page. Eleven people rode it down and the conductor let them keep the stubs.

The agency closed on 30 June 1958 and after that the building did one thing: it held freight until somebody came for it. Fertilizer came in on the north platform from 1961, and the co-op put up its own building on the far side in 1974 and did not need the freight room any more.

That is why the name changed. A building that only handles freight is a freight house, and by about 1965 nobody under forty called it the depot. The ball field beside it was first mowed for ball in 1974 and it took the name with it, and it has kept it. The Town of Cobb has mowed that field since, which is the only reason there is one.

The roof over the freight room went in the winter of 1985-86 and Verity Rail did not repair it. By the summer of 1987 the west end was open to the weather and children were getting in through the door track, which is how these things get decided.

In September the Company wrote to the fire company and offered the building for a training burn. The letter is in the scrapbook. It is four sentences and three of them are about the Company accepting no liability.

The burn was on the Saturday morning, 17 October 1987. Our own fire company had it, Marchfield came over with the aerial and Ashkettle brought water. It was lit at 9:40 and it was down by half past eleven. Thirty-one people watched from the field. Somebody counted them and wrote the number on the back of the photograph.

Four things came out before it went: [b]the station sign[/b], the freight room door track, the ticket window grille, and the stove out of the waiting room. The stove is at a house on Creek Road. We know which house.

blocks.caption: 17 October 1987, a few minutes after ten. Taken from the third base side by Doris Kittle, who was president twice and who had the only camera anybody thought to bring. The roofline you can see through the smoke is the co-op building and it is still there.

blocks.text: What is left on the ground

items: About ninety feet of the concrete platform edge along the north side of the ball field. It is the thing people sit on.
The stone foundation at the west end, two courses of it, under the burdock. You will not find it in July.
The scale pit. The township filled it with gravel in 1990 after a child got down into it and could not get out on his own.
Four bolts in a line where the order board mast stood. If you know they are there you can find them in about a minute. If you do not, you will not.
Cinders. The whole strip drains better than the rest of the field and it is the first part dry in the spring, and that is why the outfield is laid out the way it is and not square to the road.

blocks.body:
The sign is eight feet long, black letters on white, and it says COYNE FLATS. It is in the hall on the wall over the coat hooks and it has been since 1988.

The [url=synth://verityrail-preservation.org/]Verity Rail Preservation Society[/url] in Marchfield has asked for it twice, in 2002 and again in 2006, and both times the meeting voted to keep it. The 2006 vote was 7 to 4 and the minute says nothing else about it.

We lent it to them for their open house in September 2004 and it came back with a chip out of the bottom edge under the S. That is not why the vote went the way it did, whatever has been said in both directions since.

The Society does good work and their archive is better than ours by a distance. If you want the paper on this line, that is where the paper is. Their [url=synth://verityrail-preservation.org/archive]archive index[/url] is on their site and the item to ask for is A-002, which is the 1918 valuation map. Sheet 11 is this end.

The Association has 31 photographs of the building. Nine of them are the same three-quarter view from the crossing, taken between 1955 and 1980 by four different people, and the way you date them is by the cars. There are two of the inside and both of them are the freight room. There is not one of the office, which is the one everybody asks for.

Marion Teale had the scrapbook from 1994 to 2003 and she is the reason any of it is usable. She got the photographs out of three shoe boxes and onto card and wrote on the back of every one of them in pencil, and where a caption on this page is any good it is hers and not ours.

There is also a minute and a half of moving picture of the burn on [url=synth://clipvault.tv/]ClipVault[/url], put up by somebody we have not been able to identify. It is the only film of the building we know of and we would like to know who has the rest of that tape.

blocks.text: The end of the line, and what people get wrong about it

blocks.body:
The last revenue movement over the branch ran on [b]Friday 14 March 2008[/b]. It was three loaded cars of corn off the elevator east of Marchfield, billed to the river terminal at Steuben. That elevator is a mile and a half out of Marchfield and ten miles from here. [b]The last train did not come to Coyne Flats.[/b]

The last car in to this end was a covered hopper of dry fertilizer on 4 October 2007, and nobody took a photograph of it, and the man who signed for it says he does not remember it particularly.

We are putting it plainly because people here say the last train came down to the end of track, and four of us drove up to Marchfield on the Saturday to stand at the crossing and watch it go, and both of those things being true at once is how a thing gets into a book wrong in about ten years.

The abandonment was made final in September 2008 and the rail came up during 2009. The county has been talking about a trail on the bed since the spring. The Association has no position on it and has been asked for one twice.

Other people's pages on this line: [url=synth://forums.verityrail.org/]the Verity Rail forum[/url], which has been quiet since the line went and which has the photographs of the last day at Marchfield; and [url=synth://wiki.gridfall.net/]the Gridfall Wiki[/url], which has the branch written up with the dates and which is right, as far as we can check it.

[b]Changed 12 February 2006.[/b] We had the building down as 1899 from 2002 to 2006. A. Pitts of the Society sent a copy of sheet 11 of the 1918 valuation map, which gives 1898, and we have changed it and thanked him.

[b]Changed 11 January 2009.[/b] We had the burn as the 18th. It was the 17th. The fire company's run card says the 17th and so does the back of Doris Kittle's photograph.

[b]Not changed.[/b] Two people have told us the last passenger train was 1954. The timetable in the case is 1949 and the Ledger notice is 30 September 1953, and 1953 is what we are going with until somebody brings us a timetable that says otherwise. We would be pleased to be shown one.

blocks.text: *** CHICKEN BARBECUE *** SECOND SATURDAY IN AUGUST *** ELEVEN O'CLOCK UNTIL IT IS GONE *** EAT IN OR TAKE OUT *** $7.00 ***

blocks.body:
The Association has cooked chicken on the second Saturday in August since 1971. The next one is [b]Saturday 14 August 2010[/b], eleven o'clock, at the hall on Sarles Road.

[b]$7.00[/b] gets you a half chicken, a roll, a cup of beans or a cup of applesauce, and a cookie. Take-out is the same price and comes in a box. There is no drink with it and there is a cooler of pop at a dollar.

We cook until they are gone and in most years that is between one and two o'clock. If you are driving any distance, come at eleven. People who come at half past one and find us packing up are not being punished, they are just late, and we have had this conversation in the parking lot most years since 1994.

blocks.caption: The line at about ten past eleven, 9 August 2008. The man at the near end of the pit is turning with a rake handle because the tongs were still in somebody's truck. 600 halves that year and gone by twenty past one.

head: TIME
rows: The pit is lit. Two bags of charcoal to start and hardwood after that. Three people, and one of them brings a chair and is not asked to do anything else.
The halves come off the truck from the processor at Tessler. They are cut and boxed there. We do not cut chicken and we are not set up to.
The kitchen starts the beans. Two roasters, both of them older than two of the people running them.
Tables out under the maples. The pop cooler is iced. The cash box comes from the treasurer's house and not before, because that is the rule and it is a good rule.
Selling starts. Two lines. Take-out on the left, eat-in on the right, and everybody joins the wrong one at least once.
Somebody is sent to Marchfield for rolls. This has happened in six of the last ten years and we still do not order more rolls.
The pit is out and hosed. Tables in. Everything back in the hall by five and the floor swept by half past.

blocks.body:
The pit is cinder block, twenty-four feet long and three courses high, built in 1971 by Harlan Ossenfort and two men from the fire company on a Sunday afternoon, out of block left over from the fire station. It has been repointed twice and the west end has settled about an inch and a half, which is why the grates do not sit level and why there is a piece of angle iron under the corner that everybody knows about and nobody has replaced.

The grates are expanded metal in six sections and each one holds sixteen halves. Halsey Machine made them in 1978 to replace the first set, which were bed springs, and which worked.

There is no roof over the pit. If it rains we cook anyway and the line stands in the hall. If it is bad we move the roasters into the entry and cook under the overhang, which we did in 1998 and again in 2006, and which is miserable, and which we will do again.

It is the poultry school recipe. There is nothing secret about it and it is on the back of the extension pamphlet that half the county has in a drawer. We are writing it out here because people ask every August and the secretary is tired of copying it onto the back of envelopes at the cash box.

[b]For ten halves:[/b]

items: One cup of cooking oil
One pint of cider vinegar
Three tablespoons of salt
One tablespoon of poultry seasoning
One teaspoon of black pepper
One egg

blocks.body:
Beat the egg first. Beat the oil into the egg, then the vinegar, then the dry. It will separate whatever you do, so stir it every single time you go to the pit.

Mop it on every time you turn and turn about every ten minutes. It is not a finishing sauce and putting it on at the end does nothing except waste it. Twelve to fourteen minutes a side over coals that have gone grey, and if you can hold your hand at grate level for four seconds the fire is right.

The recipe as printed says half a teaspoon of pepper. Harlan put in a whole one in 1984 in the middle of an argument with a man from New Carrow and nobody has taken it back out. That is the entire difference between ours and everybody else's, and we tell anybody who asks.

The barbecue is most of what the Association has. Dues bring in about $590 a year and hall rent brings in between $300 and $700 depending on how many weddings there are.

What the barbecue has paid for since 2000: the west roof slope in 2004, the furnace in 2006, the well pump twice, the mowing, the flags, the Christmas lights on the bridge rail, the cemetery, the insurance, and a thousand dollars a year into the fund that used to be the furnace fund and is now the roof fund.

Advance tickets are [b]$6.50[/b] and go out with the July bulletin. You can also get them from any officer, at the fire company's Thursday card party, and in the office at [url=synth://kroontrucking.synth/]Kroon Trucking[/url] on Sarles Road, where Bernice keeps them in the second drawer.

Advance tickets are for counting. They are not for getting in front of anybody. Everybody stands in the same line, including the officers, including the people cooking, who eat last and always have.

items: Friday afternoon. Tables out of the cellar, the pit cleaned out, the roasters up. An hour and a half with six people, three hours with two.
Saturday 5:30 a.m. Three to light and tend the pit. Bring a chair and a jacket, it is cold at that hour in August and people never believe it.
Saturday 10:00 a.m. Two on the cash box, four on the line, two in the kitchen, one on the pop.
Saturday 3:30 p.m. Whoever is still standing.
You do not have to sign up. Come. If there are too many of us we send somebody home with a chicken, which has happened twice, and both times to the same man, who now arrives at a quarter past three.
[b]1998.[/b] Rain from nine in the morning. We cooked 400 and sold 280 and this village ate chicken for a week.
[b]2002.[/b] The pop truck did not come. A man went to Marchfield with a pickup and we made more on pop that year than in any other year, which nobody has been able to explain.

[b]2003.[/b] Nothing went wrong. It is on this list because people still ask whether we cancelled after the substation fire in June, and we did not. The power was back on this end on the Monday night and the barbecue was on the 9th of August as usual and we did 560.
[b]2006.[/b] Rain again, and the propane for the roasters ran out at half past eleven. The beans that year were warm rather than hot and we charged the same price for them and said nothing.
[b]2007.[/b] The processor sent 580 halves and twenty-four of them were whole birds. They were cut in the kitchen with the bread knife by two people who did not enjoy it.

[b]2009.[/b] Ran out of rolls at 12:20 and the store in Marchfield was out of the ones we use. Forty-one dinners went out with two slices of bread instead and not one person said a word about it, which we have decided to be proud of.

blocks.body:
The hall is the Coyne Flats School, built in 1927: two rooms and a cloakroom on a third of an acre that the school district bought off the Sarles farm in 1912.

The school closed at the end of the 1960-61 year and the children have gone to Kerrin ever since. The district sold the building at auction on Saturday 14 September 1963. The Improvement Club bid $1,350 and was the only bidder, and three weeks later incorporated as the Coyne Flats Community Association so that there was somebody to hold the deed.

Marion Teale found the 1912 deed at the clerk's office in Gridfall on her own time in 2005, which is how we know the lot is a third of an acre and not a half, which is what the assessor had and had had since 1974.

blocks.caption: The main room set up for a funeral lunch, March 2007. Fourteen tables and it is tight. The wall between the two school rooms came out in 1971 and the post in the middle is what is holding the ceiling up, so it is not coming out.

rows: People in the Town of Cobb
$25, back when the key comes back
Included. Bring your own coffee and your own foil.
96 chairs, 14 tables. Included. Do not take them outside without asking, because of 2005.
You need a permit from the state and a certificate of insurance that names the Association. Two people have ever done it and both said it was less trouble than they expected.
Telephone the treasurer. She writes it in the book on the shelf, and the book is the booking. There is no other list.
Tell her. There is no fee. There has never been a fee.

items: Sweep before you go. The broom is in the cloakroom and the dustpan is behind the door.
Take your garbage with you. There is no pickup out here and the can behind the hall is for the hall.
The thermostat is set at 58 and it is set there with a screwdriver. Please do not.
The water is hard. The coffee urn has to be descaled after every use and there is a jug of vinegar under the sink for exactly that.
The back door does not latch unless you lift it. Last one out lifts it.
Two of the four burners on the range work and they are the two on the left. The oven is fine.
If something breaks, tell the treasurer. Do not fix it yourself unless you are Gerald.

rows: Maple, original to the school. Refinished 1988 and it wants doing again.
96, per the fire marshal's letter of 16 May 1998, which is in the binder.
Oil. Second hand out of a church in Halsey, in November 2006, $2,900 with the tank and the wiring.
About 340 gallons a winter, which was $680 in 2004 and $1,190 in 2008.
West slope 2004. East slope is 1927 with a patch from 1981 and it is the reason there is a fund.
Own well until 1979, county water since. The old well is capped and is under the lilac.
1984. Pumped every third year, last in 2008.
$1,146 a year, which is the largest single thing this Association pays for.
In the entry on a frame. It came out of the belfry in 1981 when the belfry was found to be holding on by habit.

blocks.body:
The east slope wants doing. Two men have looked at it and the number is $6,400, which includes taking off two layers and the chimney flashing. The fund stands at [b]$3,190[/b] in a separate account at Marchfield Savings that takes two signatures.

A thousand dollars goes into it out of the barbecue every year. On that arithmetic it is three more barbecues, unless the estimate moves, and the estimate has moved once already.

The hall was open from the Wednesday morning to the Monday night in June 2003, after the substation burned in Gridfall on the 11th. This end of the district was one of the last back on.

We had coffee going the whole time and a chest freezer running off Kroon's generator, and eleven households put what was in their own freezers into it. The Ladies Auxiliary of the fire company did two suppers here that week and would not take anything for them.

The power came back on this end at twenty past eight on the Monday night, the 16th. That is five days, and it is the five days people mean when they say it.

Nobody died in that fire. Two of the Gridfall volunteers took in smoke and were at County General in Marchfield and were home the same afternoon. We are putting that here because we have now twice read it written down otherwise, once in something printed.

The Coyne Flats Union Cemetery is on Sarles Road a half mile north of the hall. It has its own association on paper and it has had no officers since 1996, when the last treasurer died and nobody could find where he kept anything.

There is a perpetual care fund of $1,847 in a passbook at Marchfield Savings and the interest on it buys about two mowings a year. It wants eleven.

Since 1998 this Association has cut it, out of the barbecue money, and Vern does most of it on his own mower and will not take fuel money. If somebody wants to reorganise the cemetery association properly, we will hand the whole thing over the same evening and be glad to.
Officers are elected at the annual meeting on the first Monday in November for two-year terms, half of them each year. These are the officers elected on Monday 2 November 2009.
Bernice has been treasurer for eighteen years and has said at each of the last four annual meetings that this one is the last one. The Association's position is that we believe her every time.

head: COMMITTEE
WHO
WHAT IT DOES
rows: The building. Keys, furnace, the man who comes about the septic, and the list on the wall of what is broken.
Mowing, the flag pole, the two sign boards at either end of the village, and the cemetery.
The second Saturday in August. See [url=/barbecue]the barbecue page[/url].
One page, three times a year, 168 in the mail. Typed, photocopied at the co-op, folded at the March meeting.
A card and a plant to anybody in the hospital or bereaved. $140 a year and she has never once turned in a receipt late.
The president and the two longest-serving trustees
Meets in September. Has never had to meet twice.

blocks.body:
Meetings are the first Monday at seven in the hall, except July and August. Nine people is a normal month. Fourteen come in March, when the hall rates are set, and about twenty came in 2007 when there was a motion about the dues.

Nobody has stood against a sitting officer since 1994. That is not a complaint about anybody and it is not a request for sympathy. If you want an office, tell the nominating committee any time before September and they will be delighted. If nobody tells them anything they will ask the same four people again, and the same four people will say yes, and that is how it keeps going.

[b]$5 a household for the year.[/b] $3 if everybody in the house is over seventy. It has been $5 since 1996. A motion to raise it to $8 was put in 2007 and defeated 3 to 12, and the argument against was that the barbecue pays for everything anyway and the dues are really a list of who is in, which is true and which is why nobody has put the motion again.

Paid households: 118 in 2009, 121 in 2008, 126 in 2005, 149 in 1998.

rows: $4.95 a month for the space. The name is $18 a year and Chad pays for it and will not let us pay him back.

blocks.body: The books are done on paper in a ledger and they are open to any member who asks to see them, at the hall, at a meeting, with the treasurer sitting there. Two people have asked in eighteen years and both of them were satisfied and one of them apologised, which he did not need to do.

head: YEARS
NAME
rows: The Improvement Club. Five meetings a year, in his kitchen, and the minutes for those years are on lined paper in a cash book.
The last station agent. Put in the bid on the school and ran the incorporation.
The dairy on Creek Road. Got the hall wired properly in 1966.
Built the pit. Started the barbecue.
First woman president. Got the floor refinished and took the photograph of the burn in 1987.
Seven years, and the first insurance policy that was any good.
Moved to Marchfield in 2004 to be near his daughter and resigned in the same letter. Drives back every August.

blocks.body:
There is no office and there is no telephone at the hall. The way to reach the Association is to telephone an officer. The numbers are in the Marchfield book under the person's own name and we are not putting them on this page.

[b]Post:[/b] Coyne Flats Community Association, care of the treasurer, R.D. 2, Marchfield.

[b]Email:[/b] coyneflats (at) coyneflats (dot) org. It is written that way on purpose because of the programs that lift addresses off pages. It goes to Chad, who prints them and hands them to Dorothy at Christmas. If it is anything at all urgent, telephone somebody.

Other pages in this county that are worth your time, and a few that were.

The link check is supposed to be once a year and it is not. [i]It was last done in January 2011, by Chad, who took nine addresses off altogether and struck three of them through instead, because Dorothy said to leave those on so people can see that they were there.[/i]

head: SITE
rows: Where the county argues. Anything you want to know about out here, somebody on there has already answered it wrong and then been corrected by somebody who was there.
People writing the county down. The 1994 flood and the 2003 substation fire are both done properly on there with the documents attached, which is more than we manage.
The paper. We take it and we buy the barbecue notice every July, two inches, $14.
The weekly out of Milbrook. They have put our barbecue in the calendar every year since 1988 without ever being asked and without ever getting the date wrong.
Mrs. Vance's ring. See the note at the bottom of [url=/]our front page[/url] about why we are not on the list.
Short messages. Somebody put the barbecue on it in 2008 and eleven people came who had never been.
Video. There is a minute and a half of the 1987 burn on there and it is the only film of the depot we know of.
Buying and selling. The two roasters came off there in 2005 for $40 the pair and they have cooked eleven thousand cups of beans since.
The league. Our team plays Sunday mornings at the freight house field. That page is theirs and not ours and they keep it better than we keep this one.

head: SITE
rows: Marchfield. They have the paper, the caboose and an archive that is better than ours by a distance. Second Tuesday of the month and they will feed you.
Ask for A-002, the 1918 valuation map. Sheet 11 is this end of the line and it is where the 1898 on our [url=/depot]depot page[/url] comes from.
Quiet since the line went. The photographs of the last day at Marchfield are on there and so are four people arguing about what the branch was properly called.

The railroad has a site now. Their abandonment page lists the mileposts and puts the end of track at 11.6, which settles an argument we had been having in this hall about whether it was eleven miles or twelve.

head: SITE
rows: Marion Teale's page about the Blue Kestrel, the diner out on Route 62. She lives two streets over. The diner closed in 2006 and her page is still the best thing there is about it, and she is honest about the pie.
Ray Sabo in Ashkettle, on the road cut and the old quarry. He measures things himself and he says so when he does not know.
This is the one people mean when they write to us about the numbers. It is sixteen miles from here and it is nothing to do with Coyne Flats and we have nothing to add to it.
The county surveyor's account with the high water marks. The creek came into the ball field that June and stopped eleven feet short of the hall, and his marks are how we know how close it was.
Len Mabry's weather station. The nearest thing to a record of our weather that anybody actually keeps.
They brought telescopes to the ball field in October 2003 and again in 2006 and let anybody look through them, and they did not charge and they did not want anything.
The co-op. Their building here sits on the old freight platform. Dorothy Wenzel is their vice president, which she asks to have noted has nothing whatever to do with this page.

blocks.body: Two of these are our neighbours and they get a line because they have both given us more than they have ever asked for.

rows: Sarles Road. Advance barbecue tickets are in the second drawer in the office, and the generator that ran the freezer in June 2003 was theirs.
Not from here, but they have had their name on a softball shirt since 1977 and they send the milk for the coffee every August and will not invoice us for it.

blocks.body: These are left on the page on purpose. They were real and somebody made them.

rows: Put up in 2001 by a woman in Halsey who had the 1954 and 1958 class photographs scanned on it. It stopped answering in 2007. We have written twice to the address that was on it and we have no other address for her. If anybody knows where those scans went, the Association would like a copy.
The town had four pages up between 2003 and 2006 with the meeting dates and the assessment roll on them. Nobody knows who took them down. The town clerk says it was never official in the first place.
The page with the local access numbers on it. The numbers still work. The page does not.

A page somebody made in 2004. The festival is the grange's and the fire company's and it is not ours, and we say that here because we get asked about it every September and we are the only thing out here with a website.

blocks.body: If your page is in this county and it is not on here, write and we will put it on. If your page is on here and you would rather it was not, write and we will take it off the same week, or by the following Christmas, which out here is the same thing.

blocks.label: Buttons. Most of these were made by the people whose pages they go to. The ring button is the ring's own and we have left it up even though we are not in the ring.
